sections.title: Tefilat Ha-derekh and Its Meaning
sections.html:
The Sages instituted a prayer for one who sets out on a journey: 'Tefilat Ha-derekh' (the Traveler's Prayer) (Berakhot 29b). In the past, the danger of the roads came from robbers, wild animals or natural hazards; today, the main danger is from road accidents. In any case, the same prayer that the Sages instituted is suited to all kinds of dangers on the road.

The most protected place for human beings is their natural environment, that is, the settlement or the town. But when a person is cut off from his place, from his friends and neighbors, and sets out on the road, he is exposed to a certain danger. If he is attacked, there will be fewer people who can come to his aid. If he is injured, more time will pass until he is taken to a hospital (see Maharal, Netiv Gemilut Ḥasadim 5). Therefore the Sages instituted Tefilat Ha-derekh. And they instituted it in the plural, because from a spiritual perspective, disconnection from the community is the root of the danger of the road, and therefore one who sets out on the road must associate himself with the community, and thereby his prayer will be better received.

Since we are already standing in prayer before the Creator and requesting that the journey pass in peace, we add a request that God also grant success to our ways (Berakhot 29b; 30a). This is the wording of the prayer: "May it be Your will, Lord our God and God of our fathers, that You lead us in peace, direct our steps in peace, guide us in peace, and bring us to our desired destination for life, joy and peace. Rescue us from the hand of every enemy and ambusher along the way, and from all kinds of calamities that rage and come upon the world. Send blessing upon the work of our hands, and grant us grace, kindness and compassion in Your eyes and in the eyes of all who see us. Hear the voice of our supplications, for You are God who hears prayer and supplication. Blessed are You, Lord, who hears prayer." There are certain differences between the versions of Tefilat Ha-derekh, and all of them are good.

Since today the main danger of the roads is from accidents, some maintain that it is proper to mention in Tefilat Ha-derekh the danger of accidents as well, as the Ra'avya wrote (vol. 1, Berakhot 86) that one may add to the prayer the dangers particular to that road. Some say that one who wishes to add may do so. And some say that the words "all kinds of calamities that rage and come upon the world" include road accidents as well, and therefore there is no need to add to the wording that the Sages instituted. One may choose as he wishes.1

sections.title: For Which Journey Is It Said
sections.html:
The Sages instituted that Tefilat Ha-derekh be said for a journey longer than a parsa (Berakhot 30a), close to four kilometers (3.648 km).2 If the journey is shorter than a parsa, Tefilat Ha-derekh is not said, for since it is close to a settlement, presumably there is no danger in it (Rosh). There is no need to be precise in measuring the journey; rather, each person may estimate according to how it appears to him. And if there is a special danger on the road, the prayer is said even if it is less than a parsa (as explained below in halakha 4).

Some say that the measure of a parsa is meant to give us a measure of time: if the journey takes more than seventy-two minutes, which is the time it takes an average person to walk a parsa on an unpaved road, one must say Tefilat Ha-derekh. But if the journey takes less than seventy-two minutes, since the danger does not last a long time, Tefilat Ha-derekh is not said (Responsa Yabia Omer vol. 2, OḤ 14).

However, according to most poskim, the Sages' intention was to set the length of the journey for which Tefilat Ha-derekh must be said. For the longer the journey, the farther it goes from settled areas, and the more its dangers multiply. But time has no significance, for even in the time of the Sages, those riding horses covered a parsa in less than ten minutes, and the Sages did not distinguish between one who walks and one who rides, but determined that in any case Tefilat Ha-derekh is said for a journey of a parsa. Therefore, in our times as well, when we travel in fast cars, we measure the length of the journey, and if it is more than a parsa, one is obligated to say Tefilat Ha-derekh (MB 110:30, and this is the view of the overwhelming majority of poskim).

Regarding one who travels within a city, there is a doubt. On the one hand, the Sages instituted Tefilat Ha-derekh for roads outside settled places. But on the other hand, today urban areas have grown greatly, and many people make long journeys within them; main roads similar to intercity roads have even been paved within them, and the danger on them is not much less than the danger of intercity journeys. In practice it appears that although there is no obligation in this, it is good for anyone who travels within a city more than the measure of a parsa to say Tefilat Ha-derekh without mentioning God's name at its end, that is, at the conclusion of the prayer he should say: "Blessed are You who hears prayer."3

sections.title: Laws of Tefilat Ha-derekh
sections.html:
Some say that it is proper to say Tefilat Ha-derekh immediately as a person leaves his home, while he is still in the city (Ateret Zekenim and Taz 7 [?]). And according to most poskim, although after the fact one fulfills the obligation even when saying Tefilat Ha-derekh in the city, ideally it is proper to say it immediately after leaving the city, for then one begins the journey for which one is praying (Magen Avraham, Eliyah Rabba, Pri Megadim and MB 110:29).

Seemingly it would be proper to follow the view of most poskim and say Tefilat Ha-derekh after leaving the city. However, since today there is a danger of accidents within the city as well — and, as we learned in the previous halakha, it is good to say Tefilat Ha-derekh without God's name even for a journey within the city — when one intends to set out on an intercity journey, it is proper to say Tefilat Ha-derekh with God's name at the beginning of the journey in the city. And since it is preferable to say the prayer while parked, the best time to say Tefilat Ha-derekh is when a person sits down in the car in preparation for the journey.4

If one forgot to say it when setting out on the journey, then if the distance of a parsa (close to four km) still remains until his destination, he should say Tefilat Ha-derekh; and if less remains, he should say the prayer without God's name in the conclusion (SA OḤ 110:7).

A person who travels several journeys in a day need only say Tefilat Ha-derekh the first time, and have in mind in his request all the journeys he will make that day. But if he planned only one journey, and afterward changed his mind and decided to travel again, he must say it a second time. When the journey lasts several days, one must say Tefilat Ha-derekh every morning (SA OḤ 110:5).

sections.title: The Prayer on Short and Dangerous Roads
sections.html:
As we learned (in halakha 2), because of the danger on the roads the Sages instituted the recitation of Tefilat Ha-derekh, and it is explained in the Babylonian Talmud (Berakhot 30a) that if the road is shorter than a parsa, there is no danger on it and Tefilat Ha-derekh is not said for it. That is, Tefilat Ha-derekh is said for a road whose length is close to four km (3.648 km). However, a difficulty was raised against this from the words of the Jerusalem Talmud (Yerushalmi Berakhot 4:4), which established that all roads are presumed dangerous, implying that Tefilat Ha-derekh is said even for a road shorter than a parsa. And they resolved it: on an ordinary road whose length is less than a parsa there is no danger, and therefore Tefilat Ha-derekh should not be said on it; but the Yerushalmi is speaking of a more dangerous road, and therefore even if its length is less than a parsa, Tefilat Ha-derekh must be said for it (Talmidei Rabbeinu Yona, Berakhot 20b [in the Rif's pagination]; Taz 110:6). And so it was ruled in halakha: if the road is presumed dangerous, even if it is shorter than a parsa, Tefilat Ha-derekh must be said on it (MB 110:30).

Accordingly, at times when certain roads are considered dangerous due to attacks by Arab terrorists, Tefilat Ha-derekh must be said even on a road of less than a parsa. And may it be God's will that all our enemies and those who seek our lives come to an end, and that Israel dwell securely throughout all the expanses of its land.

sections.title: Must Tefilat Ha-derekh Be Juxtaposed to Another Blessing?
sections.html:
Some have raised a difficulty regarding the wording of Tefilat Ha-derekh: why does it not open with 'Barukh'? For we have a rule: any blessing that is not juxtaposed to a preceding one, that is, which is said on its own, must open with a blessing formula, namely the words "Blessed are You, Lord." And if it is juxtaposed to a preceding one, it need not open with 'Barukh,' just as the second and third blessings of Birkat Ha-mazon do not open with 'Barukh' (Berakhot 46a). If so, Tefilat Ha-derekh, which is said as a blessing on its own — why does it not open with the words 'Barukh'?

Because of this, some were stringent always to juxtapose Tefilat Ha-derekh to another blessing (Maharam of Rothenburg), and ideally it is proper to take their view into account (SA 110:6).

But if no blessing presents itself to him, he should say Tefilat Ha-derekh even without juxtaposing it to a blessing. For according to many, Tefilat Ha-derekh is not an ordinary blessing but a prayer, and consequently the rules of blessings do not apply to it. Therefore it does not open with the words "Blessed are You," it does not need to be juxtaposed to a preceding blessing, and God's kingship is also not mentioned in it, as one is obligated to mention in every blessing (Tosafot, Pesaḥim 104b; MB 110:28).

And some say that Tefilat Ha-derekh is a blessing — the Shome'a Tefila ("who hears prayer") blessing of the Amida, for at the end of Tefilat Ha-derekh we say, "Blessed are You, Lord, who hears prayer." It does not open with 'Barukh' because its principal place is in the Amida, and there it is juxtaposed to the blessings before it; therefore, even when it is said separately, as Tefilat Ha-derekh, the Sages did not change its wording. And there is also no need to mention kingship in it, that is, "our God, King of the universe," because a blessing that is juxtaposed to a preceding one relies on the kingship mentioned in the first blessing, and since kingship was mentioned in the first blessing of the Amida, there is no further need to mention kingship in the Shome'a Tefila blessing (Talmidei Rabbeinu Yona on Berakhot 1a [in the Rif's pagination]).5
